anatomy.lede: Laid out on a ship's deck, a giant squid is mostly reach: eight thick arms, two far longer feeding tentacles, and behind them a torpedo-shaped mantle that holds the organs.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: A photographed giant squid eye measured about 27 cm across, with a 9 cm pupil — the largest eyes known in any animal apart from the colossal squid's.

hotspots.label: Eight arms
hotspots.text: Each of the eight arms carries two rows of suckers, which hold prey once the tentacles have caught it.

hotspots.label: Tentacle club
hotspots.text: The two feeding tentacles end in broadened clubs. Their suckers are ringed with sharp, finely serrated chitin teeth that grip slippery prey.

hotspots.label: Mantle
hotspots.text: The muscular mantle encloses the internal organs. Measured mantles are not known to exceed about 2.25 m.

hotspots.label: Fins
hotspots.text: A pair of fins sits at the rear tip of the mantle; body length is measured from here to the tentacle tips.

senses.lede: Almost everything known about the giant squid's senses comes from dead specimens, and it centres on one organ: the eye.

senses.name: Giant eyes
senses.text: Modelling suggests that below about 600 m an eye this size could pick out a sperm whale at more than 120 m, by the glow of bioluminescent plankton the whale disturbs. Such eyes would be poorly suited to spotting small prey or mates far away.

senses.name: A modest visual brain
senses.text: An MRI scan of one male's optic lobe found a well-developed outer layer for processing images, but a relatively small inner region that links vision to movement. Its brain may not have grown in step with its huge eyes.

body.lede: Inside, the giant squid is built like other squids, only larger — with a few features that hint at life in cold, dark water.

systems.title: Blood suited to the cold
systems.text: Research on its oxygen-carrying blood suggests it binds oxygen poorly at higher temperatures, so warm water may leave a giant squid short of oxygen. That could explain why it lives in cool, deep water.

systems.title: Closed circulation
systems.text: Like other squids it has a closed circulatory system, with blood pumped through vessels rather than washing loosely around the organs.

systems.title: A terminal organ for mating
systems.text: Most male cephalopods pass sperm packets with a modified arm. Two dying males found in shallow water were seen moving a penis-like terminal organ out through the funnel, supporting the idea that giant squid transfer sperm packets with it directly.

genome.lede: A draft genome assembled in 2020 from a specimen tissue sample gave the first look at the giant squid's DNA.

findings.title: Brain-building genes
findings.text: The genome holds about 135 protocadherin genes, many in clusters. This family, linked to wiring nerve cells, is greatly expanded in cephalopods compared with other molluscs.

findings.title: Reflectin genes
findings.text: It has seven reflectin genes and three reflectin-like genes, which in other cephalopods make the light-reflecting proteins of the skin and eyes.

findings.title: Very little variation
findings.text: Mitochondrial genomes from 43 giant squid across the world showed no regional structure and exceptionally low diversity, consistent with a single, widely dispersing global species.

mind.lede: Its behaviour has been glimpsed only a handful of times, each sighting rewriting what was assumed about it.

studies.title: Attacking bait off Japan
studies.text: An automated camera at about 900 m off the Ogasawara Islands photographed a giant squid wrapping its tentacles around a baited line, showing it to be an active predator.

studies.title: Stalking a fake jellyfish
studies.text: In the Gulf of Mexico, a camera with a ring of lights mimicking a glowing jellyfish filmed a juvenile about 3–3.7 m long. It stalked the lure, seized it with its tentacles, then pulled back into the dark.

studies.title: Probably a loner
studies.text: No two giant squid have been caught together in fishing nets, which has led researchers to suggest they hunt alone.

survival.lede: Adult giant squid have very few enemies, but one of them is the largest toothed predator on Earth.

tactics.title: Early warning
tactics.text: Seeing a sperm whale's glowing wake at long range may give a giant squid time to mount a powerful escape before the whale closes in.

tactics.title: Strike from a distance
tactics.text: Its long feeding tentacles let it seize prey well away from its body, then pull it in to the arms and beak.

tactics.title: Grip that holds
tactics.text: Toothed sucker rings on the arms and clubs grip struggling fish and squid that would slip from smooth suckers.

life.lede: How giant squid mate, where they spawn and how long they live are still largely unknown; what follows is pieced together from specimens.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: A female can carry more than 5 kg of eggs — well over a million — each only about 0.5–1.4 mm long.

stages.name: Drifting young
stages.text: Low genetic variation across the oceans suggests young giant squid disperse widely, possibly as drifting larvae carried by currents.

stages.name: Rapid growth
stages.text: One study suggests giant squid may reach adult size within about three years, an extraordinary growth rate for an animal of several hundred kilograms.

stages.name: Mating
stages.text: Males mature at a smaller size than females and store sperm packets in a Needham's sac before passing them to a female.
